strengths: Provides a principled theoretical foundation: Theorem 3.4 establishes identifiability of the CMI acquisition objective under retrospective missingness (MAR, no direct effect, positivity), connecting AFA to the causal missing-data/off-policy evaluation literature in a way prior AFA work largely ignores.

Theorem 4.2 rigorously shows that the proposed sequence-modeling surrogate loss, when minimized, recovers both a Bayes-optimal predictor and a CMI-optimal (blocked) acquisition policy, giving the empirical method a clear theoretical justification rather than being purely heuristic.

The core idea of casting AFA as an in-context/meta-learning problem via an exchangeable-sequence transformer is a novel and well-motivated combination of existing threads (PFN-style Bayesian ICL and CMI-based greedy AFA), addressing a real practical gap (single-task retraining, task-specific generative models).

Extensive experimental suite spanning synthetic GP/BNN tasks, real tabular datasets (Metabric, MiniBooNE, MIMIC-IV), and MNIST, with multiple complementary uncertainty metrics (coverage, NLL, Brier, KL, AUROC) and sensible baselines (GDFS, DIME, DQN).

Thorough appendix ablations: robustness to context length and missingness rate, lookahead vs greedy policies, gradient-estimator quality vs REINFORCE and IPW baselines, and a CNP-style meta-learning ablation, which substantially strengthens the empirical case beyond the main text.
Honest and specific limitations section (untestable MAR/positivity, no cost-sensitive MDP, time-invariance restriction, scale) rather than generic boilerplate.
weaknesses: The central MAR / no-direct-effect / positivity assumptions are strong and, as acknowledged, untestable; many realistic clinical missingness mechanisms (e.g., ordering a test because a clinician suspects an abnormal but unobserved value) plausibly violate MAR, which undercuts the generality of the identifiability guarantee that underpins the whole framework.

Real-world empirical results are mixed: Figure 8 explicitly shows uncertainty-quantification gains over the MLP baseline are inconsistent on real, unseen labels, and the fully-synthetic pretrained variant (L2M-Syn) needs task-specific fine-tuning to be competitive (Fig. 14), which partially undermines the paper's central claim of eliminating per-task retraining.

Baseline implementations are modified from their original papers in ways that could disadvantage them (e.g., DIME trained with random rather than epsilon-greedy acquisition, GDFS with fixed rather than annealed temperature), raising concerns about the fairness of the head-to-head comparisons.

Precision/recall analysis (Appendix Figs. 12–13) shows the task-specific baseline is more precise at identifying truly informative features than L2M, suggesting the meta-learned policy sometimes hedges rather than sharply ranking features—an important caveat to the headline claim of superior acquisition quality that is somewhat downplayed in the main text.

Experiments are limited to small-to-medium scale tabular settings (10–20 candidate features, datasets of a few thousand samples); scalability to larger feature spaces/datasets or to a true foundation-model backbone (e.g., TabPFN) is left entirely to future work, so the foundation-model framing in the introduction is aspirational rather than demonstrated.

The task prior (BNN/GP-based data generating processes) must be hand-specified, and performance depends heavily on how well this prior matches the deployment task; the paper does not provide much guidance on how to choose/validate priors for new domains, which limits practical reproducibility outside the tested benchmarks.

The dense theoretical exposition (proofs, multiple assumptions, blocked policies, Gumbel-softmax relaxations) is not always clearly connected back to intuitive takeaways in the main text, making the paper harder to parse for readers focused on practical AFA deployment.

strengths: The paper formalizes a novel and practically important 'meta-AFA' problem, generalizing single-task active feature acquisition to a setting where a policy is learned across a distribution of tasks with retrospective, task-varying missingness, and provides a clean causal-identifiability argument (Theorem 3.4) specifying the MAR/exclusion-restriction/positivity conditions under which the CMI objective is estimable from observed data alone.

Strong theoretical grounding: the paper proves (Proposition A.2 and its meta extension Theorem 4.2) that minimizing the proposed one-step surrogate sequence-modeling loss recovers both a Bayes-optimal predictor and a CMI-optimal greedy acquisition policy, connecting the practical training objective to the stated CMI goal rather than leaving this as a heuristic.

The architecture thoughtfully adapts a transformer for AFA: removing positional encodings, introducing context/target/query token types, and designing a custom attention mask to satisfy the context-invariance and target-equivariance properties needed for valid in-context Bayesian-style inference, plus a Gumbel-softmax relaxation enabling fully differentiable end-to-end policy training.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation spanning fully synthetic GP regression, semi-synthetic classification built on real feature distributions (Metabric, MiniBooNE, MIMIC-IV), and a real-image task (MNIST), with multiple relevant task-specific baselines (GDFS, DIME, DQN) and useful ablations on context length, missingness rate, and the value of instance-wise adaptivity.

The reproducibility appendix is detailed (architecture hyperparameters, training algorithms, preprocessing, baseline configurations, compute/runtime information), and limitations (reliance on MAR/positivity, reliance on synthetic/semi-synthetic task priors, restriction to time-invariant settings) are honestly and specifically discussed.
weaknesses: The core methodological ingredients (transformer/PFN-style in-context Bayesian sequence modeling for uncertainty quantification, and greedy CMI-based one-step surrogate acquisition from Covert et al. 2023) are both adapted from existing work; the main novelty is their combination for the meta-AFA setting rather than a fundamentally new estimation or decision-making principle, which somewhat limits originality.

Empirical gains are inconsistent: the paper itself reports that 'adaptive strategies offer only marginal gains over random acquisition on some real datasets' and that real-task uncertainty-quantification improvements are 'mixed' (Figure 8), which weakens the significance claims relative to the strength of the theoretical framing.

The 'meta' tasks used for pretraining on real datasets are semi-synthetic, generated via BNN-prior label functions over real feature distributions rather than genuinely heterogeneous real-world tasks/labels; this raises concern about how well results generalize to true cross-task diversity as claimed by the meta-AFA framing (MIMIC with real labels is the only case with authentic task heterogeneity, and even there gains are modest for some outcomes such as Readmission).

All baselines (GDFS, DIME, DQN, MLP) are strictly single-task models trained from scratch; there is no comparison to any other transfer-learning or pretrained baseline that shares information across tasks, making it hard to disentangle how much of L2M's advantage stems from meta-learning/in-context transfer per se versus simply using a larger, better-regularized transformer architecture.

Experiments are limited to relatively low feature dimensionality (d=10–20) and moderate sequence/context lengths; scalability of the in-context transformer approach (compute/memory, and acquisition quality) to higher-dimensional feature spaces or larger acquisition budgets typical of many real AFA applications is not empirically investigated.

The identifiability assumptions (MAR, exclusion restriction, positivity) underlying the theoretical guarantees are strong and untestable in real retrospective clinical data; while acknowledged as a limitation, the paper does not empirically probe sensitivity to violations of these assumptions, leaving the practical robustness of the identification result unclear.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation and theoretical apparatus in the main text, and the connection between the elaborate theory and the practical experimental takeaways could be made more explicit and accessible.
